One of the problems with reddit is that with 10-20 mods on all the major subs, there are hundreds of users who are well-positioned to curate content as they see fit. If this site ever becomes big and a PR firm figures out how to get ahold of one or two key spots in a major subverse, they could effectively use that subverse to shape public perception by curating content as they see fit.

I've thought about this problem quite a bit, and I have some ideas I'd like to bring up: I think that whatever eventually becomes reddit's successor needs to limit the problem of "powermods." This could mean imposing a limit of no more than one default subverse per user, but it would be better to get rid of moderators altogehter. The job of tagging and removing inappropriate submissions could be done by group consenseus instead.

For instance, you could create a system wherein users tag submissions that they think should be removed. If the number of users who tag a submission for removal reaches some threshold (say, 50% as many removal tags as upvotes, and at least 50 removal tags overall) then the submission would be removed. It would then be up to the admins to decide if the post should go back up, but the initial "moderation" would be done by the community itself.

I think that a system such as this would be a huge improvement because not only would it be democratic rather than authoritarian by nature, but it would also remove a huge number of potential points of failure (i.e.; mods) while simultaneously removing the plausible deniability that admins on reddit have: when content manipulation occurs on reddit, the admins don't step in--even in the default subs--because of their "principle" of moderator ownership. Again, their "hands off" approach is a mechanism to ensure plausible deniability and nothing more.

If one bot was created that submitted all community-driven removals to a specific sub that users could keep track of, and another bot noted the username of the admin removing a post and the username of the post's OP, then I think you'd basically be set (you wouldn't want the content to show up with this bot, however, since presumably the reason the submission was taken down is because it violated a site-wide rule). Curious users could go to the userpage of the OP and see what they'd submitted, but the violating post would no longer be visible elsewhere.

In addition to "tagging for removal," you could have similarly user-voted flair that wouldn't actually remove the article--things like "False/May be misleading"; "out of date"; etc.

To minimize content manipulation by sock accounts, you could perhaps even edit the code to make it so that users can't log into a new account more than once every half hour (I'm not a coder, so I don't know how feasible that last part is, but it's something worth thinking about).

In any event, my thanks go to /u/Atko for creating this site and I hope it becomes what reddit could have been if it hadn't sold out to the dark side (i.e.; become a PR playground).

The minimum number of removal tags should depend on the activity of the subverse. We don't want people to be able to post child porn in their own tiny stagnant subverses, and have it stay up because only one person even goes there a week to see it and report it.

Sadly, I think mods are needed. The site is liable for its content and cannot simply allow users to post whatever they will.

The issue is with the tags, is it would become incredibly easy for PR firms, or political organizations, to do the exact opposite of what this was supposed to solve. A group from the Rhinoceros party sees an article that bashes them? Okay, create 50 accounts, and report it 50 times. Political subs would become tumbleweed grounds, because they would essentially wipe each other's posts from the site. Also, if a PR firm sees a post bashing one of their clients, they could do the same. It would essentially create one large HailCorporate website.
